messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 45

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Military Topics: Talks about military, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Vignette:
Karim is a sixty-four-year-old divorced man who came to the United States as a young adult and eventually built a career in local politics. For the past fifteen years he has served on a city council, spending his days in meetings, public forums, and back‑room negotiations. Ten years before entering politics, Karim had volunteered as a relief worker in a conflict zone in the Middle East. He does not speak of that time unless forced to, and even then only in fragments. The event that changed him occurred on an afternoon when his convoy was ambushed while distributing food in a contested district. A mortar struck the jeep ahead of him. He remembers the world flipping sideways—the metallic hiss of the shell, the deafening blast, the sight of a driver’s arm, severed, still gripping the steering wheel. Then the fire. The smell of burning fuel, burning flesh, burning rubber. He tried to pull survivors from the wreckage, but his hands found only pieces that did not fit together. For years the memory returned as exactly that: a disjointed slide show of smoke, a child’s sandal lying in a pool of oil, the weight of a man’s head lolling in his hands. And the terror—the same raw, suffocating terror he felt in that moment—would wash over him without warning, making him stop whatever he was doing, breathless, as if he were back in the heat and the noise.

When Karim returned home, he told no one what he had seen. He had come to believe that if he ever let the feelings out, he would shatter completely. So he learned to hold his emotions in a tight fist. He threw himself into work, first as a community organizer and then as a candidate, because staying busy meant he did not have to sit with himself. Silence, especially at home, became unbearable. When the apartment was quiet he felt a tightening in his chest, a certainty that something terrible was about to happen. He began checking the locks on his doors and windows twice, then three times, before he could sleep. In public he scanned every face, every doorway, every parked car. The habit was automatic: he would walk into a coffee shop and catalogue the exits, the shadows, the strangers who seemed to look at him too long. Talking to strangers became an ordeal. Every handshake, every unscheduled conversation, felt like a potential threat. He could not place why—it was not that he thought the other person meant him harm, but the act of meeting an unfamiliar gaze triggered a visceral unease, as if the stranger might suddenly become part of the fragmented memory that still haunted him.

Becoming a politician made avoidance impossible. His job required him to shake hands daily, to attend town halls where constituents debated military policy, to stand awkwardly near the grill at barbecues where the smell of charred meat reminded him of burning bodies. He developed a repertoire of strategies: he kept his face neutral, refrained from showing anger or fear, and steered conversations toward concrete tasks. When the topic turned to a new military deployment or a veteran’s benefit, he nodded but offered no opinion, then found an excuse to move to another room. The overworking was relentless. He took on extra committee assignments, stayed late at the office, scheduled back‑to‑back meetings so that there was no gap for his mind to drift. By the time he came home, he was exhausted enough to fall asleep quickly—if he first checked the locks twice and turned on the radio to break the silence.

The cost of this system was a quiet, accumulating wreckage. His wife left him after eight years of marriage because, she said, she felt like a stranger in her own home. He knew she was right: he had never let her see the fragments, had never explained why he flinched when the smoke alarm went off or why he insisted on sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants. After the divorce he lived alone, and the solitude intensified his scanning and his checking. He found himself listening to the silence in his empty house, straining for the sound of a footstep that should not be there.

Three months before his intake appointment, Karim attended a city council hearing on a proposal to rezone a lot near a factory that occasionally released a burnt, chemical odor. Before the vote, a resident—a retired military officer—stood up and spoke passionately about the need to protect the community from industrial hazards. His words turned to the sacrifice of soldiers in recent overseas campaigns. Karim felt his jaw lock. He did not hear the next sentences; his ears filled with a high‑pitched whine, and the burnt smell from the factory seemed to have entered the room. He excused himself, walked to the restroom, and stood gripping the sink, struggling to breathe. The terror had returned—as vivid as the day of the attack, flooding him, disjointed images cascading behind his eyes. For the first time in years, he could not distract himself out of it.

That night he found himself online, searching for a therapist who specialized in trauma. He made the call because he was afraid of what might happen next: a panic attack during a televised debate, a complete breakdown that would end his career. What he hoped for, though he could barely admit it, was that someone might help him fit the pieces together so that the smell, the silence, and the strangers would stop feeling like the prelude to an explosion. He had spent decades policing his inner world, and he was exhausted.
